newsitem.title: USA: U.S. criticizes Israel's housing move.
newsitem.headline: U.S. criticizes Israel's housing move.

text.p: The United States criticised Israel's decision on Wednesday to build new Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem, but analysts expected Washington to avoid a major confrontation with the Jewish state on the issue.
"The decision taken today further complicates an already complicated situation," said a White House spokesman, David Johnson.

Defying U.S. objections and Palestinian warnings of a wave of violence, Israel approved the building of thousands of new Jewish homes in East Jerusalem. Palestinians saw the move as an attempt to cement Israel's hold over the entire city.
Johnson said the U.S. view had been communicated to the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who visited President Bill Clinton at the White House two weeks ago.

State Department officials said they were "disappointed" at a move out of line with the spirit of cooperation Israelis and Palestinians showed in last month's accord putting most of the West Bank city of Hebron under Palestinian control.
"Today's decision by the Israeli government to build housing at Har Homa is not a step that will build trust and confidence," department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"Frankly, the United States would have preferred a different decision. We would have preferred that this decision not have been taken," Burns told a news briefing.

But Burns warned against any attempt by Palestinians to express their grievances through violence. "The United States, obviously, would like to see calm in the occupied territories, in Jerusalem and throughout Israel," he said.
The spokesman said he expected the issue to come up when Palestinian President Yasser Arafat visits Washington next week for talks with Clinton and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

Despite the criticisms, analysts said the main U.S. priority was to keep the Middle East peace process moving forward and they doubted that Washington would do anything to seriously alienate Netanyahu.
"I don't think they're going to have a confrontation with him over this," said Alan Makovsky of the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a private think-tank.
"I think there's understanding for the political capital that he's used up and his need to acquire more with his coalition."
Several analysts said Netanyahu's decision appeared to be intended to recoup the support of right-wingers angered by Israel's concessions in the Hebron deal.

The United States has long disapproved of Israeli settlements. In statements scrutinised by Israeli officials for nuances invisible to outsiders, it has described them at various times as an "obstacle" and a "complicating factor" in the peace process.
But the Clinton administration has been criticised by retired officials such as former Secretary of State James Baker for failing to take firm action against Israel.
Administration officials respond that since Baker left office in 1992 Israel and the Palestinians have begun a peace process that needs to be nurtured at all costs.
Palestinian officials, however, called on the United States to intervene.

"The United States is the sponsor of this peace process and everybody knows that continuing building settlements is not going to help the peace process to go forward," said Said Hamad, deputy head of the PLO office in Washington.
"I hope that President Clinton and the administration will ask Mr Netanyahu to stop all these settlements."
